sections.h2: What is different about selling a house in Garden City?
sections.html:
Garden City requires a certificate of occupancy whenever a home is sold, and that inspection sets the real timeline for a sale here. The city is a small western suburb in Wayne County, about 15 miles west of downtown Detroit, covering 5.87 square miles. A seller who understands the inspection step early can plan the closing around it instead of being surprised by it.

The notes below cover that step, the city's housing numbers, the permit rules that affect repairs, and the taxes that follow a transfer.

sections.h2: How did Garden City get its layout and its name?
sections.html:
The city takes its name from the English garden city idea. Most early home sites were cut into one-acre plots so a family could grow its own fruit and vegetables. Garden City became a village within Nankin Township in June 1927 and a city six years later. Most lots today are far smaller, some only 40 by 135 feet.

The population jumped from 9,012 in 1950 to 38,017 in 1960 and peaked at 41,864 in 1970. The 2020 Census counted 27,380 residents. Local landmarks include the site of the first Kmart, which opened in 1962 and has since been demolished, and Henry Ford's honeymoon cottage, moved here from Dearborn in 1952. Downtown centers on the corner of Ford and Middlebelt Roads.

  • The 1950s and 1960s building boom produced most of the housing, so many houses are now more than 60 years old.
  • Lots as small as 40 by 135 feet leave little room for additions or large outbuildings.
  • Ford Road and Middlebelt Road are the main corridors for commuting and errands.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show for Garden City homes?
sections.html:
Garden City is a city of owners, with homeowners holding roughly four of every five housing units. The figures below come from the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates.

The population estimate is down 4.1% from the April 2020 base, so sellers should not count on a rising number of buyers moving in from outside the city. Pricing to the condition of the home matters more than waiting for demand to arrive.

sections.h2: How does the Garden City certificate of occupancy work for a seller?
sections.html:
Any time a property is going to be sold or has been sold, the city requires a certificate of occupancy before the new owner occupies it. The Building Department schedules the inspection, which takes place Monday through Thursday, with a morning window from 9 a.m. to noon and an afternoon window from noon to 4 p.m. The department's FAQ lists a $200 fee, payable when the inspection date is booked, and says the certificate is good for one year.

The city warns that spring and summer are the busy season, and that a seller may wait three to six weeks for an inspection. A seller who needs a fast closing should book the inspection the day the contract is signed, or earlier. The Building Department number is (734) 793-1650.

  • Book the inspection as soon as the home is listed or under contract.
  • Fix visible safety items first, since a failed inspection means a reinspection and more waiting.
  • Ask the Building Department what a December or January inspection date would mean for a closing in the same season.

sections.h2: Which repairs need a permit in Garden City?
sections.html:
A permit is good for six months, and all inspections must happen inside that window. Roof, windows, exterior doors, siding, gutters and kitchen or bathroom remodels need a building permit. Water tanks, furnaces, air conditioners and generators need mechanical permits. Service panels, circuits, fixtures and hard-wired smoke detectors need electrical permits, and sewer repairs, sinks, toilets and showers need plumbing permits. Driveways, easement walks, patios and porch caps fall under a flatwork permit.

Sheds under 200 square feet need no building permit but still need a flatwork permit for the slab. Homeowners who live in the house may pull their own permits, while anyone paying a contractor should have the contractor pull them, at the same cost. Ask the Building Department whether any open permit on the address could affect the certificate before you list.

sections.h2: What happens if the house is a rental?
sections.html:
Garden City runs a rental certification program through its Ordinance Department at the police department, reachable at (734) 793-1748. Rental certifications run three years, and the owner must recertify before the term ends. A seller who rents the house out should confirm the certification is current and tell the buyer whether tenants will stay.

A buyer who plans to keep the house as a rental should ask the Ordinance Department how a transfer affects the existing certification.

sections.h2: What taxes and filings follow a Garden City sale?
sections.html:
The county transfer tax is 55 cents per $500 in a county with under 2,000,000 residents (MCL 207.504), and the state tax is $3.75 per $500 (MCL 207.525). The seller is liable, and the tax goes to the county treasurer within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523).

On a $168,800 sale that works out to roughly $1,460 in combined tax, with the title company showing the exact figure. The buyer files a Property Transfer Affidavit with the city assessor within 45 days, and taxable value resets to the state equalized value the year after the transfer (MCL 211.27a). Residents wondering how a buyer's first tax bill will compare can ask the city assessor for the parcel's numbers.

sections.h2: Which sale route makes sense for a Garden City house?
sections.html:
A small, well-kept house on a standard lot can sell on the open market, but the inspection wait and buyer financing both add time. A house that needs work, comes from an estate, or has a tight deadline often suits an as-is sale better.

  • List when the house is in good repair and you can wait through the inspection queue.
  • Sell as-is when repairs would be needed to pass the certificate of occupancy and you prefer to let the buyer handle them.
  • Ask any as-is buyer who is responsible for the inspection fee and for any repairs the inspector requires.

Compare offers on the net you keep after transfer tax, prorated taxes and any credits, and get the closing date in writing.

faqs.q: Is a certificate of occupancy required to sell a house in Garden City?
faqs.a: Yes. The city requires one whenever a property is sold, and the new owner cannot occupy the home without it. The Building Department at (734) 793-1650 schedules the inspection.

faqs.q: How long does the Garden City inspection take to schedule?
faqs.a: The city says spring and summer sellers may wait three to six weeks. Booking early, and avoiding peak months where you can, shortens the wait.

faqs.q: What does the Garden City certificate of occupancy cost?
faqs.a: The city's FAQ lists a $200 fee, paid when you book the inspection, and a certificate valid for one year. Ask the Building Department to confirm the current fee.

faqs.q: Does a Garden City sale reset property taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer's taxable value resets to the state equalized value in the calendar year after the transfer under MCL 211.27a, and the buyer files a Property Transfer Affidavit with the assessor within 45 days.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Garden City house that has failed an inspection?
faqs.a: You can sell it, though the certificate of occupancy has to be issued before the new owner moves in. Some sellers make the repairs, and others sell as-is and let the buyer complete them and request the reinspection.
